analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The House never acted on it: introduced and referred to committee on January 3, 2019, the bill got no committee or floor action and died when the Congress ended January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The FairTax would repeal the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and replace them with a 23% national sales tax on all new goods and services, collected mostly by the states. Every family of lawful residents would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on purchases up to the poverty line, and the IRS would lose all funding after 2023. It would also repeal the estate tax entirely and leave purchases made for investment or business purposes untaxed. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any committee action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains would go to the highest-income households: investment purchases would be untaxed, so returns on wealth would never be taxed, and the estate tax on large inheritances would disappear. Businesses would gain from the repeal of payroll taxes and an administration credit for collecting the tax. Low-income families would be partly shielded by the monthly poverty-line rebate.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, effective January 1, 2021.
Leaves purchases made for business or investment purposes untaxed, so income from wealth and capital gains would not be taxed at all under the new system.
Pays registered sellers an administration credit of the greater of $200 or one-quarter of 1% of the tax they remit, and exempts business purchases from the sales tax.
Gives every family of lawful U.S. residents a monthly rebate equal to the tax rate times the federal poverty guideline for their family size, paid by the Social Security Administration.

analysis.who_pays: Middle-income households that spend most of what they earn would pay the 23% tax on nearly everything they buy new, while their income taxes and paychecks' payroll deductions would end. Social Security and Medicare would lose their dedicated payroll-tax funding and instead draw from general revenue, subject to future annual appropriations. The estate tax repeal also reduces revenue that general-fund spending — including the rebate itself — must replace.

drawbacks.text: A 23% tax would apply to the use or consumption of essentially all new goods and services in the United States, raising the price of everyday purchases.

A consumption tax falls hardest on households that spend most of their income, so middle-income families would bear a larger share of the burden relative to income than wealthy households, whose investment income would go untaxed; the rebate offsets the tax only up to the poverty line.
Repealing the estate and gift tax would eliminate the only federal tax on very large inherited fortunes.

Repealing payroll taxes ends the dedicated funding stream for Social Security and Medicare; the bill would instead allocate general sales-tax revenue to the trust funds, making their funding dependent on yearly budget decisions.
No funding is authorized for the Internal Revenue Service after fiscal year 2023, leaving enforcement of the remaining federal taxes to the states that opt to administer the sales tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would genuinely simplify life for wage earners — no income tax filing, no payroll withholding — and the monthly rebate would protect the poorest families from the sales tax. But the trade it offers is steep for the middle class: the taxes that fall most on work and wages disappear, while the taxes that fall most on wealth (capital gains and the estate tax) disappear too, and the replacement tax hits every new purchase at 23%. The distributional effect runs from middle-income consumers toward the top of the income scale, and it would make Social Security and Medicare funding hostage to annual budget fights. Whether the stated 23% rate would actually replace current revenue is disputed; if it fell short, the shortfall would fall on general spending or require a higher rate.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote on it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Rob Woodall introduced the FairTax Act of 2019 in the House on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the Congress.
33 House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing changed, everyone with a stake in the existing tax code kept it: high-income households continued to pay current-law rates on investment income and estates rather than receiving the larger cut this bill would have given them, and the IRS, the income tax, and payroll-tax funding for Social Security and Medicare all continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households kept the existing tax code

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were House Republicans and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action on it for two years.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate and gift tax and leaves investment purchases untaxed, so income from wealth would escape federal tax entirely while a 23% tax lands on everything everyone buys new. The wealthy would pay tax only on what they personally consume.

Payroll taxes on their workers would be repealed and business purchases would be untaxed, and sellers get an administration credit (at least $200, or 0.25% of tax remitted). They would take on collection duties, including bonds and segregated accounts for large sellers.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and zeroing out IRS funding after 2023 would eliminate the annual filing obligation that sustains the tax-preparation business. Consumers would no longer need paid help filing returns.
States that opt in would administer and collect the federal sales tax and keep a 0.25% administration fee, expanding their role in federal tax collection.

The bill taxes financial intermediation services, subjecting banking and insurance transactions to the sales tax, while repeal of the income tax removes taxes on capital income and financial instruments themselves.
